content: The influence of migration on the transmission of leprosy was thoroughly examined during the discussion. Factors that generally affect transmission were also considered applicable to migration between countries. These insights can be utilized to address the factors or circumstances that drive migration in the context of leprosy elimination and to mitigate the risk of migration disrupting transmission interruption and achieving the goal of leprosy elimination. Dr. Pemmraju presented a detailed framework for the control, elimination, and eradication of neglected tropical diseases (NTDs), including leprosy. The definitions used in this context were as follows: 1. Control: This refers to the deliberate reduction of disease incidence, prevalence, morbidity, and/or mortality to a locally acceptable level. Continued intervention measures are required to sustain this reduction. 2. Elimination as a Public Health Problem: This term applies to both infection and disease. It is defined by achieving measurable global targets set by the World Health Organization (WHO) for a specific disease. For leprosy, this was defined as a registered prevalence of less than one case on treatment per 10,000 population. It was believed that transmission would cease once this threshold was reached. However, continued actions are necessary to maintain these targets and further interrupt transmission. The process of documenting elimination as a public health problem is called validation. For leprosy, no formal validation process was developed, as the indicator could be determined through straightforward mathematical calculations. Most countries have achieved this benchmark at the national level, though some are still working toward achieving it at sub-national levels. 3. Elimination of Transmission (Interruption of Transmission): This is defined as the reduction to zero of the incidence of infection caused by a specific pathogen in a defined geographical area, with minimal risk of reintroduction, as a result of deliberate efforts. Continued actions may be required to prevent the re-establishment of transmission. In leprosy, since infection cannot be unequivocally determined, the absence of new autochthonous child leprosy cases for at least three years is considered a proxy indicator for transmission interruption. 4. Elimination of Disease: This is defined as zero new autochthonous leprosy cases (all ages) in a defined geographical area for three consecutive years. This definition is not absolute, as sporadic new cases may continue to occur due to the long incubation period in some individuals. Continued surveillance is required for at least ten more years to detect any sporadic autochthonous cases in the community. Sporadic cases should be unrelated. If non-sporadic cases occur after three years of zero leprosy, the situation reverts to pre-elimination status. The process of ascertaining elimination is called verification. 5. Eradication: This refers to the permanent reduction to zero of a specific pathogen, with no risk of reintroduction, as a result of deliberate efforts. The process of documenting eradication is called certification. Eradication implies the global absence of the disease. However, due to zoonotic transmission pathways, eradication may not be feasible for leprosy at this time. Dr. Zaw Lin shared lessons learned from the WHO South-East Asia Region regarding validation and verification of other NTDs. He referred to key documents, including the generic framework for control, elimination, and eradication of NTDs and the process of validating the elimination of kala-azar as a public health problem. The principles for validation, verification, and certification include preparation, submission, assessment, feedback, and acknowledgment of dossiers, as well as post-validation activities. Dr. Vivek Lal presented concepts, definitions, and indicators specific to leprosy elimination. Key terms were defined as follows: Autochthonous Case: A leprosy case presumed to have acquired the infection through local transmission in the reporting area. This definition accommodates cases detected in individuals who are not residents of the area where they were diagnosed. Population at Risk: Individuals in a leprosy-endemic area who have resided for at least six months in close proximity to an untreated leprosy case. Persons Requiring Leprosy-Related Interventions: Individuals affected by leprosy who need diagnostic services, treatment, care during and after treatment, rehabilitative support, or assistance for related disabilities or mental health problems. This also includes those requiring chemoprophylaxis. The elimination pathway for leprosy is divided into three phases: elimination as a public health problem, elimination of transmission, and elimination of disease. These phases are generally sequential, though in jurisdictions with small populations, elimination as a public health problem may not precede transmission interruption. Due to the long incubation period, there may be many years between these phases. Proposed indicators to assess transmission interruption and disease elimination include: Child Proportion Among New Cases: The percentage of new autochthonous child cases (<15 years old) among all new autochthonous cases detected in a defined period. This indicator reflects recent transmission. New Child Case Detection Rate: The number of new child leprosy cases detected in a given period relative to the child population in the area. This is expressed per million children and serves as a proxy for leprosy incidence among children. Number of New Autochthonous Child Cases Detected: The absolute number of new autochthonous child cases detected in a given population during the reporting year. This indicator is useful for forecasting multidrug therapy (MDT) requirements for children. Age at Detection of Leprosy: The age of an autochthonous new leprosy case at the time of diagnosis. An increase in mean age at detection and a shift toward older age groups suggest progress toward transmission elimination. Seroprevalence of Anti-M. leprae PGL-1 IgM Antibody Among Children: The percentage of children (5–7 years old) testing positive for this antibody. This indicator reflects recent transmission but is still in research mode and not yet generalized. Proportion of Cases with Multibacillary (MB) Leprosy Among New Cases: The percentage of new cases with MB leprosy among all new cases detected. An increase in MB proportion may indicate declining transmission. Proportion of New Autochthonous Cases with a Known Leprosy Case in the Family: The percentage of new leprosy cases with a family member diagnosed with leprosy within the past ten years. This indicator highlights familial transmission risk. Indicators related to disease elimination include the new case detection rate and the new case detection rate for autochthonous cases only. These rates are expressed per million population and reflect the disease burden relative to the population in the area or country.
